In [[finite geometry]], '''Lam's problem''' is the problem of determining if a [[Projective_plane#Finite_projective_planes|finite projective plane]] of order ten exists.
The order ten case is the first theoretically uncertain case, as all smaller orders can be resolved by purely theoretical means.<ref>{{cite journal
 |last=Hall
 |first=Marshall Jr.
 |title=Finite Projective Planes
 |journal=[[American Mathematical Monthly]]
 |volume=62
 |issue=7P2
 |pages=18–24
 |year=1955
 |doi=10.2307/2308176
 |jstor=2308176
 |mr=0073214
 |author-link=Marshall Hall (mathematician)
 |quote=The first critical value of <math>n</math> is <math>n=10</math>. A thorough investigation of this case is currently beyond the facilities of computing machines.}}</ref>
Lam's problem is named after [[Clement W. H. Lam]] who experimentally determined that projective planes of order ten do not exist via exhaustive computational searches.<ref name="lam1991">{{cite journal
 |journal=[[American Mathematical Monthly]]
 |title=The Search for a Finite Projective Plane of Order 10
 |last=Lam
 |first=Clement W. H.
 |volume=98
 |year=1991
 |issue=4
 |pages=305–318
 |doi=10.1080/00029890.1991.12000759
 |mr=1103185
 |url=https://www.maa.org/programs/maa-awards/writing-awards/the-search-for-a-finite-projective-plane-of-order-10
 |author-link=Clement W. H. Lam
|url-access=subscription
 }}</ref>

== Introduction ==

A finite projective plane of order <math>n</math> is a collection of points and lines such that
* any two points define a unique line,
* any two lines meet at a unique point,
* there are exactly <math>n+1</math> points on every line, and
* there are exactly <math>n+1</math> lines through every point.
A consequence of this definition is that a projective plane of order <math>n</math> will contain <math>n^2+n+1</math> points and <math>n^2+n+1</math> lines.
The incidence relation between points and lines may equivalently be described using an [[incidence matrix]].  In this context a projective plane of order <math>n</math>
is equivalent to a <math>(n^2+n+1)\times(n^2+n+1)</math> [[Matrix (mathematics)|matrix]] with <math>\{0,1\}</math> entries such that every row and column has <math>n+1</math> ones
and the inner product between any two rows or columns is exactly <math>1</math>.

Using the incidence matrix representation, Lam's problem is equivalent to determining if there is a way of placing 0s and 1s in a <math>111\times111</math> matrix such that there are exactly eleven 1s in each row and column and any pair of
rows share a single 1 in the same column.<ref>{{cite encyclopedia
 |title=Lam's Problem
 |encyclopedia=[[CRC Concise Encyclopedia of Mathematics]]
 |edition=3rd
 |year=2005
 |last=Weisstein
 |first=Eric W.
 |publisher=CRC Press
 |isbn=9780849319464
 |author-link=Eric W. Weisstein
}}</ref>

[[Clement W. H. Lam|Lam]] considered studying the existence of a projective plane of order ten in his PhD thesis but was dissuaded by his thesis advisor [[H. J. Ryser]] who believed the problem was too difficult.<ref name="lam1991" />

== Resolution ==

Edward Assmus presented a connection between projective planes and [[coding theory]] at the conference ''Combinatorial Aspects of Finite Geometries'' in 1970.<ref>{{cite report
 |title=Algebraic Theory of Codes II
 |date=15 October 1970
 |last1=Assmus
 |first1=Edward F. Jr.
 |last2=Mattson
 |first2=Harold F. Jr.
 |chapter=On the Possibility of a Projective Plane of Order Ten
 |institution=Air Force Cambridge Research Laboratories
}}</ref>
He studied the code generated by the rows of the incidence matrix of a hypothetical projective plane of order ten and derived a number of restrictive properties that such a code must satisfy.
In particular, the [[enumerator polynomial]] of the code is completely determined by the number of words of [[Hamming weight|weights]] 12, 15, and 16 in the code.

Over the next two decades a number of computer searches showed that the hypothetical code associated with the projective plane of order ten does not contain words of weights 15,<ref>{{cite journal
 |title=On the Existence of a Projective Plane of Order 10
 |date=1973
 |last1=MacWilliams
 |first1=F. J.
 |author-link1=Jessie MacWilliams
 |last2=Sloane
 |first2=N. J. A.
 |author-link2=Neil Sloane
 |last3=Thompson
 |first3=J. G.
 |author-link3=John G. Thompson
 |journal=[[Journal of Combinatorial Theory|Journal of Combinatorial Theory, Series A]]
 |volume=14
 |pages=66–78
 |doi=10.1016/0097-3165(73)90064-2
 |mr=0313089
|doi-access=free
 }}</ref> 12,<ref>{{cite journal
 |title=The Nonexistence of Ovals in a Projective Plane of Order 10
 |date=1983
 |last1=Lam
 |first1=C. W. H.
 |author-link1=Clement W. H. Lam
 |last2=Thiel
 |first2=L.
 |last3=Swiercz
 |first3=S.
 |last4=McKay
 |first4=J.
 |author-link4=John McKay (mathematician)
 |journal=[[Discrete Mathematics (journal)|Discrete Mathematics]]
 |volume=45
 |pages=319–321
 |doi=10.1016/0012-365X(83)90049-3
 |mr=0704249
 }}</ref> and 16<ref>{{cite journal
 |title=The Nonexistence of Code Words of Weight 16 in a Projective Plane of Order 10
 |date=1986
 |last1=Lam
 |first1=C. W. H.
 |author-link1=Clement W. H. Lam
 |last2=Thiel
 |first2=L.
 |last3=Swiercz
 |first3=S.
 |journal=[[Journal of Combinatorial Theory|Journal of Combinatorial Theory, Series A]]
 |volume=42
 |pages=207–214
 |doi=10.1016/0097-3165(86)90091-9
 |mr=0847551
 }}</ref>—which implied that it must contain words of weight 19.
Finally, Clement Lam, Larry Thiel and Stanley Swiercz used about three months of time on a [[Cray-1|Cray-1A]] supercomputer to show that words of weight 19 are also not present in the code.<ref>{{cite journal
 |title=The Non-existence of Finite Projective Planes of Order 10
 |date=1989
 |last1=Lam
 |first1=C. W. H.
 |author-link1=Clement W. H. Lam
 |last2=Thiel
 |first2=L.
 |last3=Swiercz
 |first3=S.
 |journal=[[Canadian Journal of Mathematics]]
 |volume=41
 |issue=6
 |pages=1117–1123
 |doi=10.4153/CJM-1989-049-4
 |mr=1018454
|doi-access=free
 }}</ref>
This resolved Lam's problem in the negative.
Their result was independently verified in 2021 by using a [[SAT solver]] to generate computer-verifiable certificates for the correctness of the exhaustive searches.<ref>{{cite conference
 |title=A SAT-based Resolution of Lam's Problem
 |date=2021
 |last1=Bright
 |first1=C.
 |last2=Cheung
 |first2=K. K. H.
 |last3=Stevens
 |first3=B.
 |last4=Kotsireas
 |first4=I.
 |last5=Ganesh
 |first5=V.
 |conference=[[AAAI Conference on Artificial Intelligence]]
 |pages=3669–3676
 |url=https://ojs.aaai.org/index.php/AAAI/article/view/16483
}}</ref>
